title: Multimodal Conversational AI: A Survey of Datasets and Approaches
extended_summary:
This paper surveys research on multimodal conversational AI, with the goal of defining the problem space and organizing the technical methods needed to build conversational agents that can use and generate multiple modalities such as text, images, audio, video, and dialogue history. The authors argue that current conversational systems are limited because they rely mostly on language, whereas human conversation is naturally multimodal. They formalize multimodal conversational AI as an optimization problem and introduce a taxonomy of five subproblems: representation, fusion, translation, alignment, and co-learning.

The paper does not study an educational intervention, learners, or classroom implementation. Instead, it reviews datasets and model approaches across areas such as multimodal question answering, image-grounded dialogue, video question answering, action recognition, and navigation/dialogue tasks. Examples discussed include VQA, VisDial, Image-Chat, AVSD, SIMMC, and HowTo100M, along with representative model families such as factor graph attention, TRANSRESNET, and MMV.

The main conclusion is that while substantial progress has been made on component tasks, existing datasets and methods make simplifying assumptions that limit their ability to model real multimodal conversation. The authors emphasize the need for richer datasets, better handling of long-term dialogue dependencies, and stronger multimodal co-learning methods to move toward more natural conversational AI. This paper is therefore a conceptual and survey contribution rather than an empirical study of ChatGPT or any educational use case.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a survey/theoretical paper, not an empirical study of ChatGPT or any educational intervention. It does not present original causal or correlational evidence on middle school mathematics achievement.
impact_tier_rationale: No direct impact on student outcomes is reported. The paper is background synthesis only, with no measured effect on achievement or related educational outcomes.
